annotations.text:
(Recommended) Hero A · axis: split copy-left + one portrait + credential pill row.
Why: it is the live HeroV3:b lineage measured down from ~649px to 375px at 1440 with every element kept (portrait, both CTAs, four pills, availability pill), so nothing has to be re-approved; the copy stays on the #0f3d2c scrim because that is what holds the clay H1 span at 3.6:1 (the capture hero-v3b-1280 shows the same panel).
Trade-off: one portrait of one bird sits next to the claim "6 Birds Available Now", so the inventory is asserted rather than shown.
Open question (critique pass): Hero B answers exactly that gap, naming four birds with their live prices (Evie $1,500, Roys $2,300, both verified against dist/index.html and data/price-matrix.json), and it stays inside the hero band at 389px measured. Its recorded penalty is smaller than it reads: Hero-B-Mobile runs 857px against Hero-A-Mobile 819px, a 38px difference. Whether the honesty of a shown inventory beats the zero re-approval cost of the shipped lineage is a breeder decision, not a measurement.
Open question (critique pass): the three hero artboards each pair with a different counter treatment (A the 4-up ledger, B the 2x2 tiles on the warm bed, C the inline ribbon), so a reader comparing the heroes is also comparing three counters. Holding one counter constant across all three would isolate the hero axis.

Hero B · axis: full-bleed dark scrim + 2×2 photo grid.
Why: the for-sale heroes that already ship (hero-dna-1280, hero-eggs-1280) pair the claim with a photo grid, and four named tiles put real inventory beside the CTA; grid measures 389px, inside the 350-400 band.
Trade-off: four above-the-fold images cost LCP budget, and at Mobile the hero runs 857px before the counter is reached.

Hero C · axis: mosaic metrics, stats column + inventory mosaic.
Why: the three-column rhythm reads the fastest of the three (358px grid, shortest of the trio) and puts the four proof numerals inside the hero where the eye already is.
Trade-off: those four numerals are the counter's own stats, so C only works if the counter strip below is dropped or restated; run as drawn, the page says 12+ / 100% / $1,500 / 24h twice.

(Recommended) Counter A · axis: 4-up ledger, hairline rules, clay numerals.
Why: it is the live strip (counter-home-1280) tightened, so zero copy risk on the page's highest-traffic surface; the measured problem on this homepage was hero height, not the counter, and 172px desktop is the shortest 4-up of the three.
Trade-off: its separation is the minimum layout-hero-counter-separation allows (tone shift plus a 1px rule), so any later edit that drops the border re-breaks the gate.

Counter B · axis: 2×2 tiles on the #f6efe8 bed with a 3px forest→clay top bar.
Why: rules/design.md names this exact marker as the for-sale cluster's shipped separation, so the seam is unmistakable and survives edits; the side-by-side numeral and label reads as four statements, not four decorations.
Trade-off: 234px desktop and 354px at Mobile, the tallest of the three, for the same four facts.

Counter C · axis: inline ribbon, numerals and labels on one line, horizontally scrollable at Mobile.
Why: 126px desktop and 120px at Mobile, it costs the least vertical space of any option and keeps the four facts on one reading line directly under the hero seam.
Trade-off: the numerals drop to 24px and stop reading as claims, and at Mobile the fourth stat is off-screen until the reader scrolls the ribbon sideways.

(Recommended) Dial A · axis: card tone.
Why: this is the shipped .tdial geometry on /timneh-african-grey-for-sale/ and /congo-african-grey-for-sale/ (196px card, 64px ring, .74rem rows, always-visible tag pill), so it is measured rather than proposed, and its numerals #6b625a on white read 5.9:1, the highest of the three. The 2026-07-23 density pass that shrank these rows to .7rem with the tag hidden was rejected by the breeder in one line: I can hardly read the text or click.
Trade-off: a near-white card on a cream page has the least separation from the body, so it leans entirely on the 1px border and the warm shadow to read as an object.

Dial B · axis: card tone.
Why: numerals #9fc7b0 on aviary #234f3b measure 5.0:1 and the dark block separates from the cream page without needing a border, which is why the hand-raised page ships it. Geometry is untouched; only the palette moves.
Trade-off: a dark 594px block in the left gutter competes with the hero and the footer for weight, and the two contrast pairs must never be crossed. The light card's #6b625a on #234f3b is unreadable. The active row sits on a lighter #2e5c48 tint where #9fc7b0 falls to 4.11:1, so the active numeral is #c3ded0 (5.36:1); that third pair is part of the variation.
Open question (critique pass): the tag pill reproduces the shipped .tdial .tag exactly, a clay-ink fill with white text, but at eighteen rows the tag column carries more visual weight than the labels it annotates. Retinting the tag on the dark card would read better and would diverge from the component that ships.

Dial C · axis: grouping.
Why: the homepage rail carries 18 sections under four named parts. Ungrouped, rows 07 to 18 read as one undifferentiated block, the same failure the mobile bottom sheet already solved by naming the parts.
Trade-off: four part headers add 91px to the card (685px against 594px) and duplicate the part signal already carried by the always-visible tag pill.

(Recommended) Rail A · axis: chip treatment.
Why: hardening skill 1b is a recorded breeder rejection (a bottom-pinned in-page nav interferes with the page's bottom view) and the banked fix is a rail at the TOP, sticky under the 96px header. Single-line pills are what every sibling for-sale page already ships, and the rail costs zero taps: the active section is on screen at all times, where the sheet costs two.
Trade-off: one line shows about three of eighteen labels at 390, so it is only honest if scroll-spy pulls the active pill into view, and it spends 62px under the header on every screen.

Rail B · axis: chip treatment.
Why: the stacked two-line chip is the hand-raised page's own signature and keeps number and label both legible instead of squeezing them onto one line. Raised here to 46px tall with 10px gaps, because the live chips are 42px with 6px gaps and sit under the tap-target floor.
Trade-off: two lines make each chip taller and wider, so the bar eats about 66px of vertical space and shows fewer labels per screen than Rail A.

Rail C · axis: disclosure.
Why: the sheet is the only pattern that shows all four part names at once on a 390 screen, which is why it is what ships on the homepage today. Refined here into part chips plus wrapped 44px section pills instead of one long vertical list.
Trade-off: it costs two taps before any navigation happens, it covers the content it is navigating, and its trigger sits at the bottom of the screen, the placement 1b records the breeder rejecting for the rail.
Open question (critique pass): the Sections trigger and the Reserve a Bird button are both clay fills. They never appear together, because the sheet replaces the trigger, so invariant 10 is not broken as drawn. On a real page that also carries a section CTA the trigger would be the second clay fill on screen, and demoting it to forest is the call to make then.

(Recommended) Table A · axis: mobile stacking.
Why: at 375 the four live tables split two ways. table-tblc is the only one that already stacks to data-label cards, and it is the only one of the four where every cell is fully readable with no horizontal scroll: table-others-375 clips the whole "Best for" column off the right edge of the screen, and table-mvf-375 fits only by breaking cells to one or two words per line, so "Often a touch more talkative and a bolder mimic" reads down five lines. Stacking every row into a card reproduces the one pattern that already works here, needs no JavaScript, and keeps all three or four cells of a row visible at once.
Trade-off: it is the tallest mobile answer of the three (Congo vs Timneh runs about 3,400px), so side-by-side comparison becomes vertical scrolling instead of a glance.

Table B · axis: mobile disclosure.
Why: table-cmp is the one live table that already ships a Congo/Timneh tab toggle, and table-cmp-375 is readable at 375 where its untabbed siblings are not, so the pattern is proven on this site rather than borrowed. Tablet and desktop keep the classic table with the row-label column pinned by position:sticky so it stays on screen while the value columns move, with overflow-x as the secondary affordance only.
Trade-off: one column at a time means a buyer cannot weigh male against female, or Congo against Timneh, without a tap, and the toggle needs JavaScript, so with scripts off the page falls back to the scrolling table the breeder rejected.

Table C · axis: verdict emphasis.
Why: three of the four tables already carry a verdict the classic layout buries in the last column. Congo vs Timneh has an Edge column that names Timneh on three rows, Grey vs Other Species tints the African Grey row, and Rearing Paths badges hand-raised as the Top pick. The verdict card lifts that call into a forest strip under the two mini-columns, and the zebra ledger at tablet and desktop tints only the cells the source table actually marks.
Trade-off: Male vs Female marks no winner at all, so its cards carry no strip and the variation buys nothing on that table, and it is the tallest mobile stack of the three at Congo vs Timneh, about 3,700px.

table-mvf · live on / (homepage), section 11b, under the heading "Should You Choose a Male or Female African Grey?". In table-mvf-375 and in the breeder's screenshot "what buyers ask about.png", three text columns are squeezed into 375 and the cells break to one or two words a line. The "Telling them apart" row spans both value columns and has no per-column answer, so any variation has to handle it as a full-width note.

table-others · live on / (homepage), section 11c, under the heading "How Does an African Grey Compare to a Macaw, Cockatoo, or Amazon?". This is the worst of the four on a phone: in table-others-375 and in the breeder's screenshot "african vs otherrs table.png" the fourth column, "Best for", is cut off at the right edge, so the reader never sees the answer the row exists to give. The African Grey row is the only one the source tints.

table-cmp · live on /congo-vs-timneh-african-grey/, section S6, under the heading "How Do Congo and Timneh Greys Compare Side-by-Side?". Twelve rows and four columns, the widest of the four, and the only one with a named verdict column (Edge). Its mobile answer is already a Congo/Timneh tab toggle, which is why table-cmp-375 reads cleanly while its siblings do not; the breeder's screenshot "table e desktop.png" is the desktop state.

table-tblc · live on /hand-raised-african-grey-parrot-for-sale/, section 02, under the heading "The Three Rearing Paths, Side by Side". It already stacks to data-label cards at 375 and is the one table of the four with no readability defect, so it sits here as the control; the breeder's screenshot "handraised table.png" is the desktop state. Its "Top pick" badge on hand-raised is the only explicit winner mark among the four.

Faq A · axis: grouping.
Why: the breeder's own screenshot of this section is filed as "faq section-too long", and the measurement agrees: the live accordion runs 2009px at 1280 and 2404px at 375 for twenty-one questions with one answer showing. Grouping into three named topics puts the whole set on one screen at 966px, the shortest of the three, and still holds every question in the markup.
Trade-off: a reader who does not recognise a topic label has to guess which tab their question sits behind, and two thirds of the section is hidden on arrival, so the tabs carry counts to say what is inside.

Faq B · axis: grouping.
Why: no tap is needed to read anything, which is the one thing an accordion cannot offer, and it still comes in under the live section at every width (1700 vs 2009 at Desktop, 1990 vs 1997 at Tablet, 1699 vs 2404 at Mobile).
Trade-off: it buys that by dropping card body copy to 12.5px, the smallest on this canvas, and at 768 it clears the live height by only 7px, so any answer the breeder lengthens later pushes it back over.

(Recommended) Faq C · axis: disclosure.
Why: the four questions opened by default are the four the live page already answers first and the four the shipping and pricing sections repeat: documentation, cost, nationwide shipping, DNA sexing. On Mobile, where the complaint is sharpest, that state is 1162px against the live 2404px, less than half, with no topic label to decode and no tab to pick. All twenty-one stay in the markup for a reader and for a crawler.
Trade-off: the seventeen behind the control are one tap further away than in Faq A, and once opened the Desktop state is 1836px, only 173px under the live section.

Shipping A · axis: presentation.
Why: the two tiers are the content invariant, and two equal photo cards are the only layout here that gives them equal weight; each price sits on its card head, above the body copy, in the two figures a buyer is scanning for.
Trade-off: it needs a second real photograph, so the Home Delivery card leans on our home-delivery van image; if that image is ever retired the card falls back to a second crop of the crate photo.

(Recommended) Shipping B · axis: presentation.
Why: the live section already ships a five-step flow strip under the copy, so the timeline is the treatment the page has proven; folding it into the section removes the duplicate and lands the two tiers where the strip ends, which is where a reader looking for a price arrives. Measured on this canvas it is second shortest at both widths: Desktop 1,034px against C 968 and A 1,097, Tablet 1,065px against A 1,033 and C 1,223. An earlier draft of this note claimed it was shortest at Tablet; A is, by 32px.
Trade-off: four nodes plus two end cards is more structure than two tiers strictly need, and it reads left to right, so at 390 it has to become a vertical list and gains about 470px.

Shipping C · axis: presentation.
Why: it is closest to what ships today, a photo beside the copy, so it is the cheapest to adopt, and it is the shortest artboard on this page at Desktop (724px) because the photo column absorbs the height the tier rows would otherwise add.
Trade-off: only one photo earns a place, so Home Delivery is described but never shown, and at Tablet the stack puts a 300px image above the fold before the H2 is read.
